newsitem.title: UK: British stores start flying in food to beat French strike.
newsitem.headline: British stores start flying in food to beat French strike.

text.p: British supermarket group J. Sainsbury said on Tuesday it booked two cargo planes to bring in fresh produce from Spain to circumvent road blocks in France by truckers calling for improved working conditions.
"We have booked two cargo planes arriving on Wednesday," a spokeswoman said.
The planes will be carrying courgettes, broccoli and oranges from Spain to supply the group's British supermarkets but extra costs will not be passed on to customers.

The consignments are the first set up by a major British food retailer to circumvent the strike, although other chains are considering alternative routes to beat the blockade by truckers, who are calling for improved working conditions.

Tesco, Britain's leading supermarket chain, also said on Tuesday it was considering flying in food from Spain, a major source of fruits and salad ingredients, in order to circumvent the blockade, which is in its ninth day.
In a statement, the company said that "unless conditions change rapidly by mid-week we will have to consider taking the action of flying this produce into the UK."
"Our suppliers are having trouble getting their trucks through the blockade," produce buyer Peter Durose said in the statement.

Striking truck drivers have set up 176 road blocks in France in a protest for wage rises, shorter working hours and early retirement, hampering the transportation of goods across the English Channel into Britain.
"Little is moving...and food will start to go off in the lorries...it's a very difficult situation," Tesco said.
Sainsbury, Tesco's arch-rival, has already been using alternative shipping routes to bring goods from mainland Europe into Britain.

Safeway, which said it was experiencing problems transporting some citrus fruits and other produce from Spain, said it was looking at alternatives including air, train and boat from Santander in northern Spain, to bring in supplies.
The big four British supermarkets all said there were no major product shortages at the moment but added that difficulties could emerge if the dispute continues much longer.
Tesco said it hoped that there would be "no extra cost" for customers in flying in the food.
Spain is a major source for British supermarkets for fruits, lettuce and salads during the British winter when indigenous supplies wither.
But value-for-money supermarket group ASDA Plc said air freighting in supplies would be a last resort.
"If the strike does start affecting our supplies, we will use alternative routes but air freight would be a last resort, we would want alternatives to be cost-effective," a company spokeswoman said.
ASDA has not been affected by the blockade so far but is exploring alternative transport routes, she added.
She said that the most likely route for ASDA supplies would be by land to an alternative European port and thence to Sheerness in eastern England.
